description: We're an international team based in Mozambique bringing together expertise in engineering, data science, finance, design and research.  We share a passion for building creative and functional solutions capable of solving problems.
summary:
IRIS (Integrated Remote Intelligence for Spaceflight) is a tablet web app that detects early signs of Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome (SANS) during long missions. SANS is caused by microgravity, can start without symptoms and may persist after return; in NASA data, 81% of astronauts assessed (52 of 64) showed at least one SANS-associated eye finding.

Between formal exams, IRIS lets astronauts run a five-minute self-check: near-vision acuity, an Amsler grid for central distortion and four symptom questions. Each new result is compared with the astronaut's own pre-flight baseline, not a population average. A rules engine, calibrated with simulated reference ranges built from published OCT data, turns the trend into a simple green, yellow or red light and tells the astronaut what to do next, including when to alert the flight surgeon.

Built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, IRIS works fully offline, keeps data on the device, supports Portuguese and English and offers voice guidance. It supports remote clinical decisions but never replaces diagnosis.

This matters because missions to the Moon and Mars will be longer than ever, and communication delays rule out real-time care. IRIS gives crews earlier warning and doctors better context, turning occasional eye exams into continuous, personalised surveillance.
details:
IRIS – Intelligent monitoring of astronaut vision during spaceflight

What it does

IRIS is a web platform that helps astronauts monitor their own vision during a mission and supports the early detection and follow-up of Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome (SANS). It is a monitoring and decision-support tool, not a diagnostic device: IRIS organises the evidence, flags changes and sends recommendations, while interpretation always stays with the flight surgeon and medical team.

How it works

Pre-exam questionnaire. Before each test the astronaut answers 9 short questions (spacecraft stability, lighting, symptoms, sleep, eye discomfort, recent exercise or EVA, medication, vision correction). IRIS uses the answers to judge whether conditions are suitable and whether the result can be trusted.

Quick vision tests (about 5 minutes). A near visual acuity test, one eye at a time, with letter lines that get progressively smaller, and an Amsler grid where the astronaut marks any bent lines, spots or gaps. The camera measures the distance between the face and the screen (40 cm and 33 cm) and warns if the astronaut is too close or too far.

OCT readings (optional). When an on-board OCT device is available, the astronaut can record the retinal thickness values it measures, with signal quality and an optional exam image, and IRIS compares them with their history. OCT is recommended but not required: when no OCT data is available, IRIS still works with the rest of the data, meaning the questionnaire, the acuity and Amsler tests, the test conditions and the astronaut’s history.

Reliability assessment. Each result is shown with the conditions under which it was taken: readiness, spacecraft motion, glasses, distance and lighting. IRIS compares spacecraft motion with the motion of the screen and marks tests taken during a motion event as “limited conditions”.

Comparison with a personal baseline. Every result is compared with the astronaut’s own pre-flight baseline and previous tests, and classified in levels (green – routine, orange – review advised, red – clinical priority).

Continuous history. A mission timeline shows OCT, acuity, Amsler, symptoms and spacecraft events from pre-flight to post-flight, and a trend chart tracks retinal thickness in both eyes against a reference range.

Recommendations sent to the astronaut. IRIS doesn’t just show a score; after every test it tells the astronaut what to do next.

After each result: a clear “What to do next” list matched to the result level. For example, repeat the quick tests in 2 to 3 days, use the spare reading glasses, or, for a priority change, tell the flight surgeon now and follow the approved holding plan if there is no contact with Earth.

Every day: a personalised piece of advice on the home screen, based on the astronaut’s latest results, with the date of the next recommended test.

Alerts and notifications: changes that need medical review are listed as alerts, and the astronaut is notified when something needs an answer before the next test, such as a detected spacecraft motion event.

To the medical team: the report for each session is sent automatically to Earth and the medical team, marked as priority when needed.

General guidance: “Essentials on board” gives eight practical tips for eyes and body (scheduled tests, artificial tears, eye protection, exercise, hydration, sleep, radiation protocol) and a golden rule for when to contact the flight surgeon immediately.

Voice features for hands-free use. In microgravity the astronaut may need one hand to cover an eye or hold on, so IRIS can be used by voice.

Voice answers: with the microphone on, the astronaut reads the letters of the acuity test aloud and says commands such as “next” or “all straight” instead of tapping. Speech recognition runs offline in the browser, so it works without an internet connection.

Voice guidance: with “Voice on”, the test instructions are spoken aloud.

Voice works alongside touch, so the astronaut can switch at any time, and the app warns when a device makes voice answers less reliable.

Astronaut profile. Official medical data (read-only, provided by the medical team) and personal settings such as reminders, text size and reading glasses.

Benefits and intended impact

Gives crews a simple, repeatable way to track vision between formal medical exams, which matters more as missions go further from Earth and real-time medical support becomes limited.

Reduces false alarms and missed changes by recording the context of every test, not just the score.

Turns results into action, with recommendations the astronaut can follow immediately.

Does not depend on specialised equipment: OCT readings improve the picture when available, but monitoring continues without them.

Works offline, with no dependence on a cloud server or a connection to Earth.

Gives the medical team a structured, longitudinal record per astronaut, with reports sent automatically and marked by priority.

Spacecraft motion is already used to qualify test results; other mission variables such as CO₂, radiation, lighting and mission duration are planned as future inputs.

NASA data and science behind it

NASA Human Research Program – 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight: the basis for choosing the problem (altered gravity → SANS).

NASA Ocular Health ISS Study (Macias et al., 2020, JAMA Ophthalmology): eye measurements from 11 astronauts before, during and after about 6 months on the ISS. We used it to calibrate our astronaut simulator and the app’s reference ranges (for example, 362 µm before flight and about +10% by day 150).

NASA OSDR OSD-583: intraocular pressure in mice after the 35-day Rodent Research-9 spaceflight. Used as supporting evidence in our pitch; it does not enter the calculations.

Tools and technologies

Design: high-fidelity prototype created in Figma; Manrope typeface.

Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The app works offline, is bilingual (Portuguese and English) and has light and dark themes.

Backend: no cloud server is required; the app runs from a local Python server. A public demo is hosted on Render.

Database: local storage on the device (localStorage), so each astronaut’s data stays on their own device.

Analysis: a rules engine written in JavaScript classifies each result, using simulated reference ranges generated by an astronaut simulator in Python with NumPy and validated with Matplotlib charts.

Voice: Vosk Browser with the small English Vosk model for offline speech recognition; ElevenLabs for the spoken test instructions.

Camera: MediaPipe Face Detection to estimate the distance between the face and the screen.

Testing: Playwright for automated end-to-end tests.

Demo video: FFmpeg.

AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) for code, text and translations.

All data in the current prototype is simulated.

Creativity

IRIS treats test reliability as part of the result. Instead of asking only “what did the astronaut score?”, it also asks “can this score be trusted?”, using the questionnaire, spacecraft motion and viewing conditions. It compares each astronaut with their own baseline rather than a generic norm, adapts to the data that is actually available on board, and is designed for microgravity: short sessions, large targets, offline voice answers and plain language.

Factors the team considered

Medical safety: IRIS never labels a result as SANS; limits are provisional until validated by a health team.

Microgravity usability: body and screen stabilisation, glare, viewing distance, limited crew time, hands-free operation.

Equipment and connectivity: everything runs on the device, OCT is optional, and there is guidance on what to do when there is no contact with Earth.

Privacy: each profile is visible only to its astronaut, data is stored locally, and official data is read-only.

Multidisciplinary team: design, software development, health sciences and economics/evaluation worked together.
